title: SIADH: Too Much Water for the Sodium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: SIADH causes inappropriate water retention, producing dilutional hyponatremia and concentrated urine. Neurologic symptoms from falling sodium are the immediate danger; treatment follows severity and cause and often includes fluid restriction, while severe symptomatic cases require urgent sodium-directed therapy with close monitoring.
recognize: Low serum sodium and low serum osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine are characteristic when other causes are excluded.
Headache, nausea, confusion, seizure, and reduced consciousness reflect worsening cerebral effects.
priorities: Assess neurologic status, fluid balance, weight, medications, and sodium trend.
Institute seizure precautions for severe symptomatic hyponatremia.
Follow the ordered fluid restriction and sodium-correction plan exactly.
assessMonitor: Trend sodium, serum/urine osmolality when ordered, intake/output, daily weight, neurologic status, and response to restriction or therapy.
interventions: Remove or treat the precipitating cause when possible.
Hypertonic saline is reserved for selected severe symptomatic cases and requires close monitoring.
medicationSafety: Overly rapid sodium correction can cause osmotic demyelination.
Some antidepressants, antiseizure drugs, chemotherapy agents, and other medications can contribute to SIADH.
teaching: Fluid restriction is prescribed therapy, not a punishment; explain the reason and practical ways to manage thirst.
delegationScope: Intake/output measurement may be delegated, but neurologic changes and sodium trends require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Encouraging extra oral fluids because the patient is thirsty despite dilutional hyponatremia from SIADH.
oneLinePearl: SIADH holds water, dilutes sodium, and threatens the brain.

title: Diabetes Insipidus: Free-Water Loss
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Diabetes insipidus causes inability to concentrate urine, leading to large volumes of dilute urine, intense thirst, dehydration, and hypernatremia when water intake cannot keep up. Replace water safely, monitor sodium and urine output, and use desmopressin when prescribed for central DI while avoiding overreplacement and hyponatremia.
recognize: Polyuria with very dilute urine and polydipsia are key clues; blood glucose is not the cause as it is in diabetes mellitus.
After pituitary surgery or head injury, abrupt high urine output can signal central DI.
priorities: Assess volume status, thirst, mental status, urine output, sodium, and serum/urine concentration data.
Replace fluids according to the plan and escalate hypotension or severe hypernatremia.
Administer desmopressin as ordered for central DI and evaluate response.
assessMonitor: Strict intake/output, frequent weight, sodium, urine specific gravity/osmolality when ordered, BP, and neurologic status.
interventions: Ensure access to water when the patient can drink safely unless a specific controlled replacement plan is required.
After pituitary surgery, report sudden polyuria rather than simply replacing every loss without evaluation.
medicationSafety: Too much desmopressin plus excess fluid intake can cause water intoxication and hyponatremia.
Desmopressin schedules are individualized; monitor for a return of polyuria and for over-treatment.
redFlags: Rapid high-volume urine output after pituitary surgery
teaching: Know the desmopressin plan, maintain appropriate fluid access, and report abrupt changes in thirst or urine volume.
delegationScope: Urine measurement may be delegated with clear thresholds; abrupt polyuria or sodium change requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Restricting water in untreated DI because the patient is urinating too much.
oneLinePearl: DI loses free water: lots of dilute urine, rising sodium, intense thirst.

title: Adrenal Crisis: Steroids and Fluids Now
bottomLine: Adrenal crisis can present with hypotension/shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, fever, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and sometimes hyperkalemia. In a severely ill patient with suspected adrenal insufficiency, emergency glucocorticoid treatment and fluid resuscitation should not wait for confirmatory testing.
recognize: Triggers include infection, surgery, trauma, missed steroids, vomiting that prevents oral dosing, and abrupt withdrawal after prolonged glucocorticoid exposure.
Primary adrenal insufficiency may cause hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia; glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency may not.
priorities: Assess ABCs, BP/perfusion, glucose, electrolytes, vomiting, medication history, and steroid dependence.
Administer parenteral hydrocortisone and IV fluids according to the emergency protocol.
Treat hypoglycemia and the precipitating illness.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, glucose, sodium, potassium, mental status, urine output, and response to steroids/fluids.
interventions: Obtain diagnostic blood work before steroid treatment when feasible only if this does not delay urgent therapy.
Use stress-dose steroid plans during significant illness/procedures for at-risk patients as prescribed.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop prolonged glucocorticoid therapy.
Patients with established adrenal insufficiency need emergency steroid education and medical alert identification.
redFlags: Known adrenal insufficiency with acute illness
teaching: Teach sick-day dosing, emergency injection use when prescribed, and wearing/carrying medical alert information.
delegationScope: Suspected adrenal crisis is unstable and requires immediate licensed-nurse/provider escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for a cortisol result before treating a crashing patient with known steroid dependence.
oneLinePearl: Adrenal crisis: do not make the patient prove cortisol deficiency before lifesaving steroids.
sourceBasis: Endocrine Society Primary Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline
Endocrine Society/ESE 2024 Glucocorticoid-Induced Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline

title: Myxedema Coma: Severe Hypothyroid Decompensation
bottomLine: Myxedema coma is extreme hypothyroid decompensation with altered mental status and multisystem slowing. Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, hypotension, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, or coma in a severely hypothyroid patient requires ICU-level emergency treatment.
recognize: A precipitating infection, MI, stroke, cold exposure, sedative use, surgery, or interruption of thyroid medication is common.
The patient does not have to be literally comatose; progressive confusion or obtundation can qualify clinically.
priorities: Assess airway/ventilation, temperature, rhythm, BP/perfusion, glucose, sodium, and precipitating illness.
Provide ventilatory and hemodynamic support and administer IV thyroid hormone and empiric glucocorticoid therapy as ordered.
Use cautious rewarming rather than aggressive peripheral heating in unstable severe hypothermia.
assessMonitor: Continuous rhythm/respiratory monitoring, temperature, glucose, sodium, mental status, BP, and response to treatment.
interventions: Treat the precipitating infection or other trigger.
Avoid unnecessary sedatives that can worsen hypoventilation and mental status.
medicationSafety: IV thyroid hormone can increase myocardial oxygen demand and requires specialist-directed dosing, especially in older adults/cardiac disease.
Glucocorticoids are often given until coexisting adrenal insufficiency is excluded.
teaching: Consistent thyroid-hormone replacement and prompt care for severe illness help prevent decompensation.
delegationScope: Myxedema coma is unstable critical care and requires immediate licensed-nurse/provider escalation.
examTrap: Using a heating pad aggressively on an unstable profoundly hypothyroid patient while neglecting ventilation and circulation.
oneLinePearl: Cold, slow, hypoventilating, confused: think severe hypothyroid decompensation.
sourceBasis: American Thyroid Association hypothyroidism/myxedema coma resources

title: Hypercalcemia: Bones, Stones, Groans, and Confusion
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Significant hypercalcemia can cause dehydration, constipation/ileus, weakness, kidney stones or AKI, confusion, and dysrhythmias. Severe symptoms require urgent hydration and cause-directed treatment while monitoring renal and cardiac status.
recognize: Common causes include primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, medications/supplements, and prolonged immobilization in selected patients.
Older adults may present mainly with weakness, constipation, or confusion.
priorities: Assess mental status, hydration, GI symptoms, muscle weakness, rhythm, kidney function, medications, and calcium supplement use.
Administer ordered isotonic fluids when appropriate and prepare for additional calcium-lowering therapy based on cause/severity.
assessMonitor: Trend calcium or ionized calcium, creatinine, fluid balance, ECG in severe cases, and response to therapy.
interventions: Promote mobility when safe and consistent with the cause/condition.
Review calcium/vitamin D and thiazide exposure with the care team.
medicationSafety: Patients with heart or kidney failure need careful fluid administration.
Digoxin toxicity/dysrhythmia risk can be more concerning in significant calcium disturbances.
teaching: Do not take extra calcium or vitamin D beyond the prescribed plan when hypercalcemia is being evaluated.
delegationScope: Routine intake/output may be delegated, but neurologic or rhythm changes require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Encouraging calcium supplements because the patient is older without noticing that the serum calcium is already high.
oneLinePearl: High calcium dries, slows, constipates, weakens, and confuses.

title: Hypomagnesemia: Rhythm and Refractory Electrolytes
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Low magnesium can cause tremor, weakness, tetany, seizures, prolonged QT, and dangerous dysrhythmias, and can make hypokalemia or hypocalcemia difficult to correct. Replace magnesium safely while finding ongoing GI, renal, medication, or nutritional losses.
recognize: Diarrhea, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, diuretics, proton-pump inhibitors in selected long-term users, and renal magnesium wasting can contribute.
Torsades risk rises when magnesium is low, especially with QT-prolonging drugs.
priorities: Assess rhythm, neuromuscular symptoms, potassium/calcium, renal function, and ongoing losses.
Use cardiac monitoring for severe symptomatic deficiency or dysrhythmia.
Administer oral or IV replacement according to severity and renal function.
assessMonitor: Trend magnesium, potassium, calcium, ECG when indicated, renal function, and symptom response.
interventions: Correct ongoing diarrhea/vomiting or medication contributors when possible.
Replace cautiously in significant renal impairment because magnesium can accumulate.
medicationSafety: Rapid/excess IV magnesium can cause hypotension and neuromuscular/respiratory depression.
Magnesium-containing laxatives/antacids can be risky in severe renal failure.
teaching: Follow prescribed replacement and report persistent diarrhea or medication use that may contribute to losses.
delegationScope: Critical magnesium values, dysrhythmias, and IV replacement reactions require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Repeatedly replacing potassium without checking magnesium when the hypokalemia will not correct.
oneLinePearl: If potassium will not stay up, check magnesium.
sourceBasis: MedlinePlus Magnesium Blood Test and Deficiency Resources

title: Metabolic Acidosis: Find the Acid or Lost Bicarbonate
bottomLine: Metabolic acidosis means primary bicarbonate reduction. DKA, lactic acidosis/shock, kidney failure, severe diarrhea, and toxins are important causes; rapid deep respirations may be compensation, so suppressing ventilation without addressing the cause can worsen acidemia.
recognize: ABG/VBG patterns show low pH with reduced bicarbonate in uncompensated or partially compensated metabolic acidosis.
Anion-gap calculation helps separate retained organic acids from bicarbonate-loss states.
priorities: Assess perfusion, glucose/ketones, renal function, GI losses, medications/toxins, respiratory compensation, and potassium.
Treat the underlying cause rather than chasing pH alone.
Escalate shock, severe hyperkalemia, declining consciousness, or respiratory fatigue.
assessMonitor: Trend pH/bicarbonate, electrolytes/anion gap, glucose, lactate when indicated, renal function, respiratory effort, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Use cause-specific fluids, insulin, dialysis, antidotes, or bicarbonate only when clinically indicated by the treatment plan.
medicationSafety: Routine bicarbonate is not appropriate for every metabolic acidosis and can create sodium/volume and electrolyte complications.
teaching: For chronic kidney-related acidosis, adhere to the individualized alkali/diet plan rather than self-treating with bicarbonate products.
delegationScope: Blood-gas collection scope varies; interpretation and unstable-patient response require licensed clinical assessment.
examTrap: Treating Kussmaul respirations as the primary problem and sedating the patient instead of correcting DKA or shock.
oneLinePearl: Metabolic acidosis: low bicarbonate, lungs compensate by blowing off CO2.
sourceBasis: National Kidney Foundation Metabolic Acidosis Guidance

title: Metabolic Alkalosis: Acid Loss or Alkali Gain
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Metabolic alkalosis is a primary rise in bicarbonate, commonly from vomiting/NG suction, diuretics, volume/chloride depletion, or excess alkali. Potassium and chloride depletion often accompany it and can increase weakness and dysrhythmia risk.
recognize: ABG shows elevated pH and bicarbonate when not fully compensated.
Prolonged gastric losses and loop/thiazide diuretics are classic exam causes.
priorities: Assess GI losses, diuretic use, volume status, potassium, chloride, renal function, and rhythm.
Replace volume/chloride/potassium as ordered when depletion is the driver.
Reduce unnecessary gastric suction losses when clinically possible and ordered.
assessMonitor: Trend electrolytes, pH/bicarbonate, intake/output, NG output, BP/orthostasis, and ECG when potassium is low.
interventions: Use the lowest effective NG suction strategy and ensure ordered replacement of losses.
Treat the underlying endocrine or medication cause when present.
medicationSafety: Diuretics can perpetuate potassium/chloride loss; medication review is part of correction.
Do not give potassium without confirming renal function and the replacement order.
redFlags: Seizure or severe neurologic symptoms in profound alkalemia
teaching: Report persistent vomiting and use diuretics/supplements only as directed.
delegationScope: NG-output measurement may be delegated; electrolyte/acid-base deterioration requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Ignoring potassium because the question is labeled as an acid-base disorder.
oneLinePearl: Vomiting loses acid—and often chloride and potassium with it.

title: Respiratory Acidosis: Ventilation Failure
bottomLine: Respiratory acidosis results from inadequate alveolar ventilation and CO2 retention. Opioid/sedative overdose, severe COPD/asthma fatigue, neuromuscular weakness, CNS depression, or airway/ventilator problems require correction of ventilation—not bicarbonate as the primary fix.
recognize: ABG shows low pH with elevated PaCO2 in acute uncompensated or partially compensated disease.
Headache, confusion, somnolence, flushed skin, and respiratory depression can accompany hypercapnia.
priorities: Assess airway, respiratory rate/effort, sedation, breath sounds, oxygenation, capnography when available, medications, and neuromuscular status.
Reverse/treat the cause and support ventilation rapidly when the patient is tiring or obtunded.
assessMonitor: Trend mental status, respiratory effort, blood gases, oxygenation, CO2 monitoring when used, and response to bronchodilation/ventilatory support.
interventions: Prepare for noninvasive or invasive ventilatory support when ordered and clinically indicated.
Use naloxone in suspected opioid toxicity according to the emergency protocol while supporting ventilation.
medicationSafety: Sedatives and opioids can worsen CO2 retention.
Oxygen should be titrated to the ordered target, but needed oxygen is not withheld from a hypoxemic patient out of fear of CO2 retention.
teaching: Use respiratory medications and oxygen exactly as prescribed and seek help for increasing drowsiness or work of breathing.
delegationScope: Respiratory deterioration and blood-gas interpretation require licensed clinical assessment.
examTrap: Reassuring yourself because the oxygen saturation looks acceptable while the patient becomes progressively somnolent from CO2 retention.
oneLinePearl: Respiratory acidosis means the patient is not ventilating enough CO2 out.

title: Respiratory Alkalosis: Hyperventilation Has a Cause
bottomLine: Respiratory alkalosis results from excessive ventilation and CO2 loss. Anxiety can cause it, but so can hypoxemia, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, pregnancy, pain, liver disease, CNS injury, or excessive mechanical ventilation—so do not label unexplained tachypnea as anxiety before excluding dangerous causes.
recognize: ABG shows elevated pH with reduced PaCO2 in acute disease.
Lightheadedness, perioral tingling, paresthesias, and carpopedal spasm can occur as ionized calcium shifts.
priorities: Assess oxygenation, chest pain, fever/infection, pregnancy, pain, neurologic status, medications, and recent ventilation changes.
Treat the cause of hyperventilation and support the patient calmly while dangerous etiologies are evaluated.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate, oxygenation, blood gases when indicated, hemodynamics, temperature, and symptom response.
interventions: Correct excessive ventilator settings only through the respiratory/medical plan.
Use calming breathing coaching for confirmed anxiety-related hyperventilation after red flags are excluded.
medicationSafety: Do not routinely use sedatives for unexplained tachypnea because they may obscure sepsis, PE, or neurologic deterioration.
complications: Delayed diagnosis of the underlying emergency
teaching: For recurrent confirmed panic-related hyperventilation, use prescribed coping strategies, but new or different symptoms still warrant assessment.
delegationScope: Unexplained tachypnea requires licensed-nurse assessment before being attributed to anxiety.
examTrap: Giving the patient a paper bag to rebreathe before excluding pulmonary embolism, hypoxemia, or sepsis.
oneLinePearl: Low CO2 is a clue—ask why the patient is hyperventilating.
